title: ChatTier.fromStr returns Optional[Self] — None on invalid string, never raises
content:
`ChatTier.fromStr(v: str)` at `internal/bot/models/chat_settings.py:144-157` returns `Optional[Self]`: it wraps `cls(v)` in `try/except ValueError: return None`. So a malformed or unrecognized tier string yields `None`, NOT an exception.

Production impact in `base.py`:
- `getChatTier` (`base.py:341-359`, returns `Optional[ChatTier]`) calls `ChatTier.fromStr(...)` at lines 354 and 357 and returns the result DIRECTLY, without an immediate null-check. So a malformed PAID_TIER or BASE_TIER string makes getChatTier return None.
- The downstream fallback chain (`base.py:262-266`) catches that None: if `chatTier is None and BASE_TIER in defaultSettings` → try fromStr again; if still None → `ChatTier.BANNED`.
- Net behavior: a malformed paid/base tier string silently resolves to the next tier in the fallback chain (ultimately BANNED) rather than erroring.

Confirmed during the `scripts/check_condensing.py` confirmation re-review (2026-07-11): the script's tier resolver uses defensive `paidTier = fromStr(...); if paidTier is not None: return paidTier` checks, which is MORE robust than production's direct-return pattern (it short-circuits correctly instead of returning None when the key is present but the value is malformed). Callers replicating tier logic should null-check the fromStr return before using it.

title: Chat settings resolution: tier-defaults layer and per-setting tier gating
content:
Production chat-settings resolution (`BaseBotHandler.getChatSettings` / context assembly in `internal/bot/common/handlers/base.py`, ~lines 255-308) is NOT a simple "defaults + DB overrides" merge. It has four layers and tier-gating:

**Layer 1 — defaults:** global + per-chat-type defaults (loaded in `HandlersManager.__init__`).

**Layer 2 — tier-defaults:** `tierSettings = cache.getDefaultChatSettings(f"tier-{chatTier}")` (`base.py:268`), keyed like `tier-paid`, `tier-base`, `tier-banned`. Loaded from `botConfig.get("tier-defaults", {})`. This is the non-obvious middle layer — scripts that omit it diverge from production. The original `check_condensing.py` bug (Gate 1 finding #4) was precisely this omission.

**Layer 3 — DB per-chat overrides, tier-GATED:** iterating `chatSettings.items()` (`base.py:281-303`), each override is conditionally included:
- Each settings page has a `minTier()` (`base.py:282`). If `not chatTier.isBetterOrEqualThan(settingTier)` AND the setting was not set by a bot owner → the override is DROPPED (`base.py:289-292`).
- MODEL / IMAGE_MODEL settings get EXTRA gating: the model's own tier (`ChatTier.fromStr(modelInfo.get("tier", ""))`) is checked, and if it exceeds the chat's tier, the override is dropped (`base.py:293-301`).

**Tier resolution** (`base.py:259-266` + `getChatTier` at `341-359`): PAID_TIER checked first (active only if `PAID_TIER_UNTILL_TS >= time.time()`), then BASE_TIER from DB settings, then BASE_TIER from defaults, finally `ChatTier.BANNED`.

Scripts/tools replicating the resolution (e.g. `scripts/check_condensing.py`) must: load global+per-type defaults, load tier-defaults (`tier-{chatTier}`), then merge DB overrides. The tier-gating of per-chat overrides can usually be approximated as a flat `dict.update()` for dry-run purposes, but the tier layer must not be skipped.

title: Agent files enumerate permitted commands in multiple sites — update all together
content:
When adding a new permitted command (e.g., `make check-docs`) to an opencode agent definition (`.opencode/agents/*.md`), the file typically has MULTIPLE sites that enumerate "permitted commands" — all must be updated together or the agent may second-guess whether the command is truly allowed:

1. **The `bash:` permission allow-list** in the YAML frontmatter (e.g., `"make check-docs*": allow`).
2. **"Hard Constraint" / "Operating Principles" prose sections** that enumerate "permitted read-only gates" or "explicitly permitted" commands — e.g., code-reviewer.md has at least two such spots: one in the Hard Constraint section ("Read-only verification commands — `make lint`, `make test`, `./venv/bin/pytest` — are explicitly permitted") and one in an allowed-usage enumeration.
3. **Methodology / verification checklist sections** that tell the agent which commands to run and when.

Concrete example: when propagating `make check-docs` to `.opencode/agents/code-reviewer.md` (2026-07-11), the developer added it to the bash allowlist AND the review methodology (step 3 quality gates), then realized the Hard Constraint prose still listed only lint/test/pytest as permitted. Without updating the prose, an agent reading the Hard Constraint might refuse to run check-docs because it "wasn't in the allowed list." So the developer went beyond the two-requested-changes scope and added check-docs to the Hard Constraint enumerations too — this was the right call for internal consistency.

Style note: bash allow-list entries can be exact-match (`"make lint": allow`) or wildcard (`"make lint*": allow`). The two agent files differ in convention — docs-writer.md uses wildcards, code-reviewer.md uses exact matches. When adding a new read-only command, the wildcard form (`"make check-docs*": allow`) is safer since it allows arguments (e.g., `make check-docs V=1`).

title: CORRECTION: Piped bash commands ARE allowed in opencode when every segment matches an allowlist pattern
content:
CORRECTION of deleted memory 2cb79249 (which incorrectly claimed piped commands fall through to deny). That memory was "inferred from pattern semantics, not verified." This is the empirically verified behavior:

**Empirical evidence (2026-07-11, in a live code-reviewer session):**
1. `ls .agents/skills | wc -l` → **ALLOWED** (returned 8). The session's allowlist had `"ls *": allow` and `"wc *": allow`.
2. `make lint 2>&1 | tail -20` → **DENIED**. The session had `"make lint": allow` (exact, no wildcard). The `2>&1` made the first segment not match the exact pattern.
3. Bare `make lint` → **ALLOWED** (exact match works for the bare command).

**Conclusion:** opencode does NOT reject piped commands wholesale. It appears to split the command on pipe `|` and evaluate each segment independently against the allowlist. If EVERY segment matches an allow pattern (considering wildcard semantics), the entire piped command is permitted. If ANY segment fails to match, the whole command is denied via the catch-all `"*": deny`.

**Key interaction with exact-match rule (memory eefc752f):** Patterns without `*` are exact-match. So `"make lint"` matches only bare `make lint`, not `make lint 2>&1`. Patterns WITH `*` are prefix/glob match. So `"ls *"` matches `ls <anything>`, and a pipe segment `ls .agents/skills` matches it.

**Impact on docs-writer.md:** docs-writer has `"ls*": allow`, `"grep*": allow`, `"wc*": allow`. So `ls … | grep … | wc -l` IS permitted (all segments match wildcard patterns). The claim at docs-writer.md:171 that this "falls through to *: deny" is factually WRONG. The guidance to use Glob/Grep tools is still sound advice (structured results are more reliable), but the stated permission-system reason is incorrect.

title: Agent definition changes (.opencode/agents/*.md) only take effect in a new session
content:
Changes to `.opencode/agents/*.md` files (frontmatter permissions, prompt text, allowlists) are loaded at session start and do NOT apply to an already-running session.

**Evidence (2026-07-11):** A code-reviewer agent was launched, then `code-reviewer.md` was committed with a new `"make check-docs*": allow` entry in the bash allowlist. When the running code-reviewer tried to execute `make check-docs`, it was DENIED — the session was still using the pre-commit permission set (which had `make format`/`make format lint` but no `make check-docs*`). The committed changes only take effect when a new agent session is started.

**Practical implication:** When iterating on agent definitions (permissions, allowlists, prompts), you must start a new session to test the changes. A running agent cannot validate its own updated definition. This is particularly important for code-reviewer/debugger agents reviewing their own config changes — they can read the committed file but cannot exercise its new permissions.

title: Config section [search-history] vs class ChatSearchHandler naming mismatch
content:
The chat-history-search feature has an inconsistent three-way naming that causes real confusion:

- **Config section:** `[search-history]` in `configs/00-defaults/search-history.toml` (key `enabled`, plus `[search-history.embeddings]` and `[search-history.defaults]`).
- **Accessor:** `configManager.getSearchHistoryConfig()` (note: "SearchHistory", not "ChatSearch").
- **Handler class:** `ChatSearchHandler` in `internal/bot/common/handlers/chat_search.py`.
- **Conditional registration gate:** `manager.py:540` — `if configManager.getSearchHistoryConfig().get("enabled", False):` wraps the `ChatSearchHandler` instantiation.

The config key is `[search-history]`, NOT `[chat-search]`. The handler class is `ChatSearchHandler`, but the config section and accessor use "search-history" naming. People (including the user) informally write `[chat-search]` — that config section does NOT exist.

When documenting or referencing the enable gate, use `[search-history].enabled` to match the code (source of truth). Verified in configs/00-defaults/search-history.toml:4 and manager.py:540 on 2026-07-11.

title: get_messages_by_ids tool: three-layer gating decision (resolved 2026-07-11)
content:

2. **`ALLOW_TOOLS_COMMANDS` (global per-chat master tools toggle):** YES, the tool SHOULD be gated on it, consistent with every other LLM tool.
3. **NOT gated on `EMBEDDINGS_ENABLED` or any embeddings/search-specific flag:** this is a pure DB lookup, available whenever chat-search is on, even when semantic search/embeddings are disabled.

**IMPORTANT CODE DRIFT (verified 2026-07-14):** The current implementation of `_llmToolGetMessagesByIds` (chat_search.py:827-937) does NOT enforce Gate 2 (ALLOW_TOOLS_COMMANDS) — the check was removed (body has no getChatSettings call, jumps Gate 1 chat-context → Gate 3 input-validation). The docstring (chat_search.py:840-841) and registration comment (chat_search.py:281-283) still claim the ALLOW_TOOLS_COMMANDS gate exists, but the code does not implement it. This is a known regression: re-add the ALLOW_TOOLS_COMMANDS check mirroring `_llmToolSearchMessages` (chat_search.py:562).

**User rationale for layer 1:** 'if some day we'll want to disable search for messages, I suggest that we'll want to disable this tool as well.'

**Array param JSON-Schema (resolved):** the `message_ids` ARRAY param should include `extra={"items": {"type": "string"}}` on its `LLMFunctionParameter` (currently at chat_search.py:289). ToolName members use UPPER_CASE Python name ↔ snake_case string value.

title: opencode permits pipes when every segment matches an allowed bash pattern
content:
**Discovery (2026-07-11):** A prior claim in `docs-writer.md` that piped bash like `ls … | grep … | wc -l` "falls through to `*: deny`" because "the pipeline only matches the first command's pattern" was FALSE. This was removed from docs-writer.md.

**Actual behavior:** opencode permits a pipe when EVERY segment in the pipeline matches an allowed bash pattern. If docs-writer allows `ls*`, `grep*`, and `wc*`, then `ls … | grep … | wc -l` IS permitted (all three segments match). A pipe is only denied when at least one segment does NOT match any allowed pattern.

**Implication for agent authoring:** When writing bash allowlists, a pipe involving commands X, Y, Z requires all three (`"X*": allow`, `"Y*": allow`, `"Z*": allow`) — not just the first command. This also means the "exact-match unless wildcard" rule (memory eefc752f) applies per-segment in a pipeline.

**Note:** The GUIDANCE to prefer `Glob`/`Grep` over piped bash remains valid — but for accuracy/reliability reasons (structured tools return countable, auditable, logged results; shell pipes are fragile due to word-splitting, exit-code masking, brittle glob expansion), NOT for permission reasons.

title: Zero-tolerance broken-link policy: no baseline caveats in agent-facing docs
content:
**Decision (2026-07-11, user directive):** Agent-facing instructional docs must present `make check-docs` as a clean pass/fail gate with ZERO caveats about pre-existing broken links. No mention of "~375 pre-existing", no "known drift", no "baseline", no "focus on new breakages." If `make check-docs` fails, agents must report ALL broken links — whether from their own edits or pre-existing.

**Rationale:** Normalizing a broken baseline (the old "~375 pre-existing broken links, focus on NEW breakages" caveat) is counterproductive — it conditions agents to tolerate broken output and the count itself becomes stale drift once links are fixed. The goal is zero broken links.

**Scope:** Applies to `.opencode/agents/*.md`, `.agents/skills/*/SKILL.md`, `AGENTS.md`. Does NOT apply to:
- `docs/llm/teamlead-memory.md` — historical session log (factual record of what was found, not a standing instruction).
- `.opencode/memory.jsonl` — durable memory storage (factual records by date).
- `tests/scripts/test_check_docs.py` — has an `xfail(strict=True)` test (`test_noBrokenLinks_inRealRepo`) that self-destructs when links are fixed; this is the legitimate transition mechanism driving toward zero.

**What changed:** Removed the caveat from 4 locations in 3 files:
- `.opencode/agents/docs-writer.md:173` (Method step 4) + `:206` (checklist: "no NEW broken links introduced by your edits" → "no broken markdown links")
- `.opencode/agents/code-reviewer.md:172` (review methodology step 3)
- `.agents/skills/update-project-docs/SKILL.md:149` (Step 8 checklist)

The `make check-docs` instruction itself is PRESERVED everywhere — only the normalizing caveat was stripped.

**Supersedes:** Prior memory `b2d67c93` which recommended "focus on NEW breakages, compare against known baseline." That approach is explicitly rejected.

title: check_docs.py non-obvious behaviors: archive source/target asymmetry, no :line verification, template placeholders
content:
Two non-obvious behaviors of `scripts/check_docs.py` (the `make check-docs` checker) that are NOT documented in doc-link-fix-campaign.md and still hold as of 2026-07-14:

**1. docs/archive/ source/TARGET asymmetry.** `docs/archive/` is excluded from scanning as a SOURCE (its own outbound links are never checked — it's a frozen historical snapshot, pruned via `_isExcludedDir` during `os.walk`), but it is **NOT excluded as a TARGET**. Links pointing INTO `docs/archive/` from other files are still validated normally — `_resolveTarget` (scripts/check_docs.py lines 297-334) only checks `resolved.exists()` with no excluded-target logic. This is intentional and load-bearing: `lib/geocode_maps/README.md:246` links to `/docs/archive/design/geocode-maps-client-design-v1.md` (verified present) and that link must resolve. Do NOT add `docs/archive/` to any 'skip targets' list.

**2. Only file existence is checked, NOT :line accuracy.** The tool strips `:lineNumber` and `:start-end` suffixes (regex `:[0-9]+(?:[-,][0-9]+)*$` at scripts/check_docs.py line 329) before checking `resolved.exists()` (line 380). It never opens the target file to verify the line number points at meaningful content. Consequence: a link like `[](internal/config/manager.py:59)` passes check-docs even if line 59 has drifted to unrelated content after a refactor. When batch-repointing broken links to moved files, stale `:line` anchors go UNDETECTED — this is why doc-link-fix-campaign.md advises DROPping stale `:line` suffixes when repointing to moved files.

(A former third behavior — docs/templates/ placeholder links — is RESOLVED: docs/templates/ is excluded via `_EXCLUDED_PATH_PREFIXES`; documented in doc-link-fix-campaign.md.)

title: Deleted/moved source files referenced in docs: wrapper.py→database.py, max_adapter.py never existed
content:
Two source-file references that appear in documentation (especially `docs/suggestions/refactoring.md`) are stale/nonexistent and must be repointed when fixing broken doc links:

**1. `internal/database/wrapper.py` — DELETED.** The monolithic `DatabaseWrapper` class (3,021 lines) was refactored away. title: Parallel agents on shared working tree produce unreliable global-state observations
content:
When two (or more) agents work concurrently on the same git working tree, each agent sees the OTHER agent's intermediate edits as they happen. This makes any observation of GLOBAL/shared state — e.g., "how many broken links total in the repo" — unreliable from either agent's perspective, because the count reflects a partially-edited tree (some links fixed by agent A, some by agent B, some not yet started).

**Encountered during:** the 2026-07-11 doc-link-fix campaign. Two parallel agents fixed ~376 broken markdown links. Each agent's TOTAL broken count was unreliable because they saw each other's intermediate working tree state. A third agent had to do a clean SERIAL verification (`make check-docs` run once, alone) after both finished to get the authoritative count (0 broken).

**Lesson:** After parallel agents finish editing overlapping areas of the working tree, always run a fresh serial verification of any shared/global metric before trusting it. Do NOT trust either parallel agent's count of global state.

title: condenseContext(returnCoverage=True) silently drops failed-batch messages — coverage indices don't span full range
content:
**Non-obvious gotcha (originally confirmed 2026-07-11; API references updated 2026-07-14 after the `returnCoverage` / index-range simplification).** `LLMService.condenseContext()` now ALWAYS returns `Tuple[Sequence[ModelMessage], Dict[int, CondensingDict]]` — there is NO `returnCoverage` kwarg anymore (removed 2026-07-13). It can silently DROP messages from its output. Dropped messages appear in NO coverage entry's `messageIds` list; the dict keys (indices into `newBody`) remain contiguous 0..N-1, but some original body messages are simply unrepresented.

**Two drop paths in `internal/services/llm/service.py` (condenseContext body-summarization loop):**
1. **Oversized single message** (~line 831-834): if a batch of `currentBatchLen == 1` still exceeds `summaryMaxTokens`, `startPos += 1; continue` — that single message is skipped, no coverage entry, no `generateText` call.
2. **Batch exception** (~line 846-852): on LLM call failure, `startPos += currentBatchLen; continue` — entire batch dropped, no coverage entry.

**Consequence for callers:** `condensedRet = retHead + newBody + retTail`, but `newBody` may represent FEWER original messages than the body held. Any caller that assumes every original body message appears in exactly one coverage entry's `messageIds` will be wrong — dropped messages are absent from all entries with NO explicit skip marker. The dict keys are always contiguous (0..len(newBody)-1), so key-contiguity is NOT a signal of completeness.

**Safe approach:** derive head/tail lengths from `len(condensedRet)` structure (`retHeadLen = len(condensedRet) - len(coverage) - keepLastN`) rather than assuming coverage covers the full body. To find which original messages were dropped, diff the union of all `coverage[k]["messageIds"]` against the original body message IDs.

**Note on obsolete fields:** the pre-2026-07-13 design used a `returnCoverage: bool` kwarg, a `CondenseBatchCoverage` TypedDict with `coveredFromIndex`/`coveredToIndex` fields, and caller-side `indexToEntry`/`indexToEntry2` parallel lists. ALL of these were deleted in the 2026-07-13 simplification and replaced by `ModelMessage.source`-based coverage computed inside `condenseContext` via `generateCondensingDict` (see ADR-019 in `docs/llm/architecture.md` and `docs/llm/memories/condensed-context-retrieval.md`).

title: Two RECOMMENDATION issues from Phase 3a fix re-review (non-blocking)
content:
**Two non-blocking issues found during re-review of the Phase 3a indexToEntry2 fix (2026-07-11, glm-5.2 code-reviewer).**

**1. base.py:971-974 — Misleading comment.** The code comment claims the empty-coverage (all-batches-fail) case "degrades to `indexToEntry[:len - keepLastN] + indexToEntry[len - keepLastN:]`, i.e. all of indexToEntry — the same as the old fallback." This is WRONG: when all batches fail, `newBody` is empty so `condensedRet = retHead + retTail` and the failed body messages are DROPPED. The formula correctly produces head+tail only (the assert at :981 still holds because `condenseCacheMessages` also drops the body), but it is NOT "all of indexToEntry." A future maintainer trusting this comment could simplify the code incorrectly. Fix: rewrite comment to "degrades to head+tail source entries (failed body dropped), matching `condensedRet = retHead + retTail`."

**2. base.py:954 — Incomplete IndexError guard.** The guard `lastCondensedMessage = dbMessageList[-1 - keepLastN] if len(dbMessageList) > keepLastN else dbMessageList[-1]` correctly handles `0 < len <= keepLastN` but still raises IndexError if `dbMessageList` is empty (the summary loop at base.py:878 `dbMessageList = dbMessageList[skippedMessages:]` can trim it to empty). This is pre-existing (old code crashed identically), but the guard is labeled as an IndexError guard and doesn't fully guard. Additionally, `lastCondensedMessage` is computed eagerly even when `coverage` is non-empty, but its only consumers are the coverage-empty fallback branches at :1016-1017 and :1034-1035 — so a non-empty-coverage run can crash computing an unused value. Fix: `dbMessageList[-1 - keepLastN] if len(dbMessageList) > keepLastN else (dbMessageList[-1] if dbMessageList else None)`, with None-guarded consumers — or compute lazily inside the coverage-empty branches only.

title: Testing condensing path: _condensingChatSettings() helper + ChatSettingsValue.toModel patch pattern
content:
To test the condensing branch of `handleRandomMessage` (Phase 3b), a new test helper pattern was introduced in `tests/bot/common/handlers/test_llm_messages.py`:

**`_condensingChatSettings()`** — extends the existing `_fullChatSettings()` with the 4 condensing-branch keys that `_fullChatSettings()` deliberately omits (CHAT_MODEL, CONDENSING_MODEL, CONDENSING_PROMPT, CONDENSING_SYSTEM_PROMPT). The model-typed values use real `ChatSettingsValue("dummy-model")` instances, but `ChatSettingsValue.toModel` is patched at class level to return `Mock()` — this avoids hitting the real LLM manager (`getLLMManager().getModel()` raises ValueError for unregistered model names).

**Integration test patching stack** (all needed simultaneously):
```python
with patch.object(EnsuredMessage, "fromDBChatMessage", AsyncMock(return_value=lightweightEM)), \
     patch.object(EnsuredMessage, "toModelMessageList", AsyncMock(return_value=[ctxModelMsg])), \
     patch.object(ChatSettingsValue, "toModel", return_value=Mock()), \
     patch("random.random", return_value=0.0):
    result = await liveHandler.handleRandomMessage(em, Mock())
```

**`_makeContextRow(messageId, username, ts) -> ChatMessageDict`** — builds minimal but complete ChatMessageDict rows for the context walk. Must include `message_id`, `username`, `date` (as datetime, not float) because `buildCondensingFields` reads all three. Rows are stored in the parallel `contextRows` list and eventually passed to `buildRandomContextDict`.

**`_lightweightContextEM()`** — returns a bare `EnsuredMessage` with empty metadata (no `randomContext`, no memories). Used as the `fromDBChatMessage` return value so the context-building loop doesn't break early (the break condition checks `eMsg.metadata.get("randomContext") is not None`).

**Key gotcha**: patching `EnsuredMessage.toModelMessageList` at class level affects BOTH the context messages (in the walk loop) AND the current message (appended after condensing). This is acceptable because the test only cares about the condense path and persisted metadata, not the final `_sendLLMChatMessage` output.

**Verification status**: This pattern is UNVERIFIED — `make test` was not run. The integration tests may need debugging.

title: Test gotcha: mock getChatMessagesSince with newest-first rows or deque double-reverses
content:
When writing integration tests that mock `getChatMessagesSince` for the `handleRandomMessage` context-building walk, you MUST provide rows in **newest-first** order to match production's `ORDER BY c.date DESC, c.message_id DESC`. The natural/intuitive way to build test rows is oldest-first (ascending timestamps), but feeding oldest-first rows to the mock causes a **double-reversal bug**: the deque's `extendleft(...)` reverses them AGAIN to newest-first instead of the expected oldest-first.

## The fix
In the test helper `_wireCondensePath` (`tests/bot/common/handlers/test_llm_messages.py`), reverse the rows before handing them to the mock:
```python
handler.db.chatMessages.getChatMessagesSince = AsyncMock(return_value=list(reversed(rows)))
```
The `rows` param is documented as chronological (oldest-first) for test-author convenience; the helper reverses to match production DB order.

## Why this matters
- `sourceRows` (the post-deque list) must be oldest-first for `buildCondensingFields` to yield `messageIds` in ascending order.
- `tillMessageId = messageIds[-1]` (newest) and `tillTS = dateRange["to"]` (max timestamp) are consistent ONLY when sourceRows is oldest-first.
- The fallback branch uses `sourceRows[0]` as the "oldest row" — correct only if oldest-first.

## ContextRows deque alignment (verified correct)
The production code uses two parallel deques:
- `contextMessages.extendleft(reversed(emittedMessages))` — preserves order within batch, reverses across batches.
- `contextRows.extendleft([storedMsg] * n)` — NO `reversed()`, but doesn't need it because all entries within a batch are identical. Across batches, both deques reverse identically, so 1:1 alignment holds.

title: P3b review: integration tests never exercise multi-emit contextRows tagging — alignment only verified for single-emit
content:
**Finding from 2026-07-11 code review (test quality gap).** The Phase 3b integration tests (`TestHandleRandomMessageCondensing` in `tests/bot/common/handlers/test_llm_messages.py`) patch `EnsuredMessage.toModelMessageList` to return a fixed `[ctxMsg]` — exactly ONE ModelMessage per row. This means the production line `contextRows.extendleft([storedMsg] * len(emittedMessages))` (llm_messages.py:983) is only ever exercised with `len(emittedMessages) == 1`, where deque alignment is trivial.

The multi-emit alignment correctness was verified ONLY by the simulation test `testAlignmentWithMultiEmitRows` (test_message_metadata.py:551-588), which hand-builds `indexToEntry` and never calls the production `contextRows.extendleft(...)` code. If the production tagging had a reversal bug, no integration test would catch it.

**Production code IS correct** (traced algebraically): because every tag in `[storedMsg] * n` is identical, `extendleft`'s element-reversal is observationally irrelevant, and the count prepended matches `contextMessages.extendleft(reversed(emittedMessages))` exactly. Both sides prepend N elements to the left, maintaining 1:1 positional correspondence even for multi-emit rows.

**Recommended fix:** Add one integration test where `toModelMessageList` is patched with a `side_effect` that returns `[ctxMsg, extraMsg]` (2+ messages) for specific rows, drive the real walk, and assert persisted `messageIds` come out deduped and in source order. This would also exercise the `messageCount` overcount defect.

**This qualifies the prior memory (id: 1bba05eb) which stated "1:1 alignment verified correct by integration tests" — that verification only covered single-emit, not multi-emit.**

title: CondensingDict tillMessageId/tillTS boundary = NEWEST (upper), not oldest — fallback was inverted
content:
Phase 3b fix (2026-07-11). `CondensingDict.tillMessageId`/`tillTS` represent the UPPER coverage boundary (the NEWEST/last covered message), NOT the oldest. This is a contract that must be consistent across all derivation and consumption sites:

- **Consumption site** `base.py:872-876`: `tillTS` is treated as an upper bound — `dbMessage["date"] > lastDT` means "newer than the summary's boundary", i.e. messages strictly AFTER the summary are skipped.
- **Path A** `_condensingDictFromCoverage` (base.py @staticmethod): derives `tillMessageId` from `messageIds[-1]` and `tillTS` from `dateRange["to"]` — both newest.
- **`buildRandomContextDict` coverage branch** (llm_messages.py): derives from newest covered message.
- **TypedDict docstring** `internal/bot/models/message_metadata.py:98-112`: documents "last covered message".

BUG: the empty-coverage defensive fallback in `handleRandomAnswer` (llm_messages.py ~line 1033-1037) used `sourceRows[0]` (oldest, since `sourceRows` is oldest-first), contradicting all three correct sites. Fixed to `sourceRows[-1]` (newest). Local variable renamed `oldestRow` → `newestRow`. The fallback branch only fires when `condenseContext` returns empty coverage (truncation/all-batches-failed), so the bug was latent.

Key takeaway: when deriving boundary markers for a `CondensingDict`, always use the NEWEST covered message, regardless of which code path. If you see `sourceRows[0]` or any "oldest" derivation, it's wrong.

title: buildCondensingFields messageCount must count UNIQUE message_ids — multi-emit pattern creates duplicate entries
content:
Phase 3b fix (2026-07-11). `buildCondensingFields(entries)` in `internal/bot/models/message_metadata.py` had an overcounting bug in its `messageCount` computation.

ROOT CAUSE — the multi-emit parallel-index pattern: callers (Path A `base.py`, Path B `llm_messages.py`) build their parallel index lists with `[row] * len(emittedMessages)` to tag EVERY emitted ModelMessage. A single original `ChatMessageDict` can emit multiple ModelMessages (via `toModelMessageList`, which prepends a `randomContext` message + per-tool messages). So the same row appears N times in the entries passed to `buildCondensingFields`. The old code did `messageCount += 1` per entry, counting the duplicated rows N times — contradicting the `messageCount` docstring "Number of original messages this summary covers."

FIX: `messageCount` for raw rows now comes from a `rawMessageIds: set[MessageId]` (unique ids), tracked separately from summary contributions. Final: `messageCount = len(rawMessageIds) + summaryCount`, where `summaryCount` accumulates `summary.get("messageCount", 0)` unchanged. `MessageId` is hashable (`__hash__` is consistent with `__eq__` for MessageId-vs-MessageId, though not mixed with plain int/str), so a set works. The `messageIds` output list is ALREADY deduped and unchanged.

Key takeaway: the `[row] * len(emittedMessages)` pattern means entries can contain duplicate message_ids. Any counting/accumulation over entries that treats them as unique-originals is wrong — dedupe by message_id first. The existing `messageIds` list dedup was already correct; only the `messageCount` counter was wrong.

Test locking this in: `testMultiEmitRowsCountUniqueIds` in `tests/bot/models/test_message_metadata.py` — entries `[{id:100}, {id:100}, {id:101}]` → asserts `messageCount == 2` (not 3) and `messageIds == [MessageId(100), MessageId(101)]`.

title: Phase 4 implemented: renderCondensedSummary — JSON renderer for condensed summaries
content:
Phase 4 of condensed-context-retrieval is now IMPLEMENTED (2026-07-11). The shared `renderCondensedSummary(data: Union[CondensingDict, str]) -> str` function in `internal/bot/models/message_metadata.py` renders condensed summaries as JSON, resolving the latent asymmetry where real user messages were JSON but summaries were raw text.

**Output JSON shape** (keys sorted alphabetically by jsonDumps):
```json
{"type": "condensed", "coveredMessageIds": [...], "participants": [...], "dateRange": {"from": "<ISO>", "to": "<ISO>"}, "messageCount": N, "summary": "<text>"}
```

**Key implementation details:**
- `CondensedSummaryKind(StrEnum)` with single member `CONDENSED = "condensed"` — deliberately separate from `MessageType` (which classifies media). Condensed is a render-only construct, structurally disjoint from real user messages.
- Mirrors `formatForLLM` exactly: builds dict, drops falsy values via `if v`, serializes via `utils.jsonDumps(ret, compact=False)`. Empty lists/0/None values are omitted (NOT emitted as null/empty).
- `coveredMessageIds`: each `MessageId` from `data["messageIds"]` serialized via `.asMessageId()` (int for Telegram, str for Max).
- `dateRange`: unix floats from `CondensedDateRangeDict = {"from": float, "to": float}` converted to ISO via `datetime.datetime.fromtimestamp(ts, datetime.timezone.utc).isoformat()` (produces `+00:00` offset). Absent → key omitted entirely.
- Legacy `str` input (old `randomContext` rows): renders `{"type":"condensed","summary":"<str>"}` with all metadata omitted (graceful degradation).
- Legacy 3-field `CondensingDict` (text/tillMessageId/tillTS only): renders summary-only since new metadata fields are absent.

**Both injection sites now emit JSON:**
- Path A (`internal/bot/common/handlers/base.py` ~line 868): `ModelMessage(role="user", content=renderCondensedSummary(condensedMessage))` — was `condensedMessage["text"]` raw text.
- Path B (`internal/bot/models/ensured_message.py` ~line 1229): `renderCondensedSummary(randomContext)` — replaced 14-line `isinstance(randomContext, str)` branching with single call. Renderer handles both `str` and `CondensingDict`.

**chat-prompt-suffix** (`configs/00-defaults/bot-defaults.toml` ~line 214-220): Russian documentation of the condensed-summary JSON shape added after `userMemories` bullet, including reference to `get_messages_by_ids` tool for fetching original messages via `coveredMessageIds`.

**Tests:** 15 new tests in `tests/bot/models/test_message_metadata.py` (11 renderer unit tests + 3 Path B integration via `toModelMessageList` + 1 Path A import-wiring test). P3b transitional tests in `test_ensured_message.py` updated to assert JSON instead of raw text. Full suite: 3191 passed, 11 skipped (baseline 3176).

**Testing limitation:** Path A (`getThreadByMessageForLLM`) requires heavy handler mocking (DB/cache/LLM service/chat settings); used lightweight import-wiring verification instead (`base.renderCondensedSummary is renderCondensedSummary`).

title: P4 code review: renderCondensedSummary verdict and findings
content:
Code review of Phase 4 (renderCondensedSummary) completed 2026-07-11 by code-reviewer agent. Verdict: **renderer is CORRECT, asymmetry is RESOLVED.** No critical defects.

**IMPORTANT finding — dangling `get_messages_by_ids` tool reference (cross-phase dependency):**
The P4 `chat-prompt-suffix` in `configs/00-defaults/bot-defaults.toml` (~line 214) instructs the LLM to call `get_messages_by_ids`, but that tool does NOT exist yet (P5 not implemented — confirmed: only `MAX_GET_MESSAGES_BATCH` constant at `internal/bot/constants.py:257`, no `ToolName.GET_MESSAGES_BY_IDS`, no handler, no registration). The suffix lives in `configs/00-defaults/` (always loaded). If P4 deploys before P5, the LLM sees instructions for a non-existent tool. Fix: ship suffix atomically with P5's tool registration, or defer the tool-reference sentence to P5. Bounded harm (no crash; model sees docs but can't act), but misleading.

**REC — `summary` falsy-drop vs "always present" contract:**
In the dict-path, `"summary": data["text"]` is inside the `if v` comprehension (message_metadata.py ~line 216). If `text == ""` (possible under condensing-model empty-completion fallback), summary is dropped → `{"type":"condensed", ...metadata}` with no summary, contradicting docstring ("always present"). This MIRRORS `formatForLLM` exactly (which also puts `"text": messageText` in the falsy-drop comprehension, ensured_message.py:1167), so "mirror exactly" goal is satisfied. Fix options: (a) hoist `ret["summary"] = data["text"]` after comprehension, or (b) soften docstring. Str-path builds dict WITHOUT filtering, so two paths disagree on empty text (moot in practice — empty str never reaches renderer due to `if randomContext:` guard at ensured_message.py:1230).

**REC — Path A wiring test too weak:**
`TestPathAWiring.testRendererImportedInBaseModule` (test_message_metadata.py:1291-1306) only checks `base.renderCondensedSummary is renderCondensedSummary` — proves import exists, NOT that injection site at base.py:868 calls it. A regression to `content=condensedMessage["text"]` would pass this test. Path B has proper integration tests (TestPathBInjectionSite + TestRandomContextReadSite). Suggestion: add `inspect.getsource` assertion or lightweight integration test.

**VERIFIED NON-ISSUE — dateRange tz consistency (plan §11 #4 resolved):**
Plan worried summaries force UTC while real messages use "their own tz". In fact, `FORCE_SQL_TIMEZONE = datetime.timezone.utc` (internal/database/utils.py:23) means `self.date` loaded from DB is ALSO UTC → `self.date.isoformat()` (ensured_message.py:1164) yields `+00:00`. Both renderers are UTC-consistent. The suffix's "(UTC)" label is accurate. No code change needed.

title: FORCE_SQL_TIMEZONE = UTC — all DB-loaded datetimes forced to UTC on read
content:
`internal/database/utils.py` line 23: `FORCE_SQL_TIMEZONE: Optional[datetime.tzinfo] = datetime.timezone.utc`

This is a MODULE-LEVEL CONSTANT that affects the DESERIALIZATION (read) path in `sqlToCustomType`. When a `datetime.datetime` is loaded from the DB and has no tzinfo (naive datetime), it is automatically assigned UTC via `data.replace(tzinfo=FORCE_SQL_TIMEZONE)` (utils.py:122-123). When it has tzinfo, it's converted to UTC (utils.py:157, 178).

**Consequence:** ALL datetimes loaded from the DB via the provider layer are tz-aware UTC. So `self.date.isoformat()` on `EnsuredMessage` (where `self.date` comes from `fromDBChatMessage` → `sqlToCustomType`) produces `+00:00` offset. This means:
- Real user messages' `date` field in `formatForLLM` JSON renders as `+00:00`.
- `renderCondensedSummary`'s `dateRange` (which also forces UTC via `datetime.timezone.utc`) renders as `+00:00`.
- Both are CONSISTENT — no mixed timezone offsets in LLM context.

This resolved the concern raised in `docs/plans/condensed-context-retrieval-plan-v1.md` §11 #4 about timezone inconsistency between real messages and condensed summaries.

Note: this is distinct from the WRITE-path convention `dbUtils.getCurrentTimestamp()` (which also returns UTC). `FORCE_SQL_TIMEZONE` covers the READ path — ensuring loaded datetimes are always tz-aware UTC regardless of how they were stored.

title: renderCondensedSummary FIX: summary hoisted out of falsy-drop (always present)
content:
Code-review fix (2026-07-12) to `renderCondensedSummary` in `internal/bot/models/message_metadata.py` dict-path.

**Bug:** The dict-path built its output via a comprehension `if v` (drops falsy values), and `summary` was inside that comprehension. When `data["text"]` was empty string `""`, `summary` was silently dropped — contradicting the design contract that a condensed summary's minimal shape is `{"type":"condensed","summary":"..."}` (a summary with no summary text is meaningless).

**Fix:** `summary` is now hoisted out of the filtered comprehension and assigned unconditionally afterward:
```python
ret = {k: v for k, v in {...}.items() if v}   # type, coveredMessageIds, participants, dateRange, messageCount — all still falsy-filtered
ret["summary"] = data["text"]                  # always present — honors the contract
```

**Contract (corrected):** `type` and `summary` are ALWAYS present in dict-path output. All other fields (coveredMessageIds, participants, dateRange, messageCount) remain subject to the `if v` falsy-drop. The str-path (legacy `str` input → `{"type":"condensed","summary":"<str>"}`) was already correct (no filtering) and was not touched.

**Regression test:** `TestRenderCondensedSummary.testEmptyTextSummaryKeyStillPresent` — passes a `CondensingDict` with `text=""` and asserts `"summary" in parsed` and `parsed["summary"] == ""`. This FAILS against the pre-fix code.

**Note:** This corrects the earlier Phase 4 memory (724792b7) which described "builds dict, drops falsy values via `if v`" without noting that `summary` is now exempt from the drop.

**General gotcha:** When using a `{k: v for k, v in d.items() if v}` falsy-drop comprehension, fields that must ALWAYS be present (per a design contract) must be hoisted out and assigned unconditionally, not included inside the comprehension.

title: Testing convention: inspect.getsource() to strengthen wiring/injection-site tests
content:
Convention established (2026-07-12, Phase 4 code review) for strengthening wiring tests where full integration testing is impractical due to heavy mocking requirements (DB/cache/LLM service/chat settings).

**Problem:** A wiring test that only asserts import identity (`module.func is func`) would NOT catch a regression where the injection site reverts to calling the wrong function or accessing the wrong field. For example, `testRendererImportedInBaseModule` asserted `base.renderCondensedSummary is renderCondensedSummary` — but if `getThreadByMessageForLLM` silently reverted to `content=condensedMessage["text"]`, the import-identity check would still pass.

**Solution — source inspection:** Add a source-inspection assertion alongside the import-identity check:
```python
import inspect   # module-top import per project rules

# in the test:
src = inspect.getsource(BaseBotHandler.getThreadByMessageForLLM)
assert "renderCondensedSummary(condensedMessage)" in src
```

This proves the injection site actually CALLS the renderer with the expected argument shape. `inspect.getsource()` returns the source of a specific method, so the string assertion is scoped to that method's body only.

**When to use:** When a wiring test can't do full integration (the target method requires too much mocking), pair the import-identity assertion with a `inspect.getsource()` + string-in-source assertion. Both are cheap and complementary — import identity catches re-exports, source inspection catches call-site regressions.

**Where applied:** `tests/bot/models/test_message_metadata.py` → `TestPathAWiring.testRendererImportedInBaseModule`, verifying `BaseBotHandler.getThreadByMessageForLLM` (base.py:868) calls `renderCondensedSummary(condensedMessage)`.

**Note:** This addresses the testing limitation noted in the earlier Phase 4 memory (724792b7): "used lightweight import-wiring verification instead."

title: Test suite root cause: ~65-68% of wall-clock is real time.sleep/asyncio.sleep blocking
content:
**Historical profiling record (2026-07-12). STATUS UPDATE 2026-07-14: the optimization is COMPLETE — see memory `6f58cec7` for the implemented result (107s → 38s). This entry is kept only as the root-cause baseline; the 'proposed, not yet implemented' framing below is OBSOLETE.**

Profiling the full test suite (3202 tests, ~107s wall-clock) revealed that approximately 65-68% of measured execution time was consumed by REAL wall-clock `time.sleep`/`asyncio.sleep` calls, NOT by computation, DB setup, or I/O.

**The dominant slow subsystems (all sleep-bound, all since fixed):**
1. `tests/lib/utils/ttl_dict_test.py` — direct `time.sleep(2)` calls to test TTLDict expiration. FIXED: in-module `fakeClock()` CM (memory `350183c0`).
2. `tests/lib/rate_limiter/test_sliding_window.py` — tests call `applyLimit()` which internally does `await asyncio.sleep(waitTime)` at `lib/rate_limiter/sliding_window.py:208` (verified line 208 still correct). FIXED: `installFakeClock` helper (memory `14c7e34c`).
3. `tests/lib/rate_limiter/test_integration.py` — same `applyLimit` blocking pattern. FIXED.
4. `tests/lib/cache/test_integration.py` + `test_dict_cache.py` — direct `asyncio.sleep` for TTL expiration. FIXED: `fakeClockContext` CM + `fakeClock` fixture (memory `836a0605`).
5. `tests/bot/common/handlers/test_chat_search.py::test_cron_self_reset_does_not_fire_on_full_batch` — production `asyncio.sleep(BACKFILL_INTER_MESSAGE_DELAY_SECS=0.1)` at `internal/bot/common/handlers/chat_search.py:450` (corrected from earlier ':410' typo; verified line 450 in current source) fires 50× per batch (`BACKFILL_DEFAULT_BATCH_SIZE=50`). FIXED: autouse class-scoped `AsyncMock()` no-op.

**Key architectural insight (still valid):** `TTLDict` and `SlidingWindowRateLimiter` read `time.time()` directly and call `time.sleep`/`asyncio.sleep` directly with no injectable clock. The rate limiter's `applyLimit()` blocking on `asyncio.sleep(waitTime)` is the design under test — it genuinely waits for the window to expire.

**Implemented optimization (was 'proposed'):** Inject a virtual clock / monkeypatch `time.sleep`/`asyncio.sleep`/`time.time` in the rate-limiter/TTL/cache/handler test files. Verified savings: ~64% (107s → 38s). See memory `6f58cec7` for the post-implementation bottleneck frontier (none sleep-bound).

title: Pytest markers are mis-targeted — genuinely slow tests carry no marker
content:
The project defines 6 custom pytest markers (`slow`, `performance`, `benchmark`, `memory`, `stress`, `profile`) in pyproject.toml, but NONE are auto-skipped and the marker system delivers ~0% time savings today (verified 2026-07-12).

**Problem:** The markers are on the wrong tests.
- `slow` = 15 tests, ALL in `tests/lib/sandbox/backends/test_docker.py` (11 Docker integration) + `tests/lib/bayes_filter/test_bayes_filter.py` performance class (4) + 1 sandbox bootstrap.
- `performance`, `benchmark`, `memory`, `stress`, `profile` = **0 tests each** (defined but completely unused).

The genuinely slow tests (rate_limiter, ttl_dict, cache — which account for ~65% of suite time) carry **NO marker at all**. Deselecting all markers (`-m "not slow and not performance and not benchmark and not stress and not memory and not profile"`) takes 108.53s vs 107.36s full run — i.e., zero improvement, within noise.

**Implication:** `make test` cannot be selectively trimmed via markers without either (a) re-marking the genuinely slow tests, or (b) fixing the root cause (see the sleep-bound profiling memory). If a fast local lane is desired, the slow tests need to be marked first.
